cited_details.statement: Automotive millimeter-wave radar (typically operating in the 77–81 GHz band) is a low-cost, weather-resilient, and reliable sensor that complements cameras and LiDAR in perception stacks for autonomous driving ([K-Radar, NeurIPS 2022](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/185fdf627eaae2abab36205dcd19b817-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html)).

However, unlike cameras and LiDAR, where deep learning has rapidly displaced classical processing pipelines, radar processing has historically lagged behind because radar signals are sparse, noisy, and lack the rich semantics of images ([Deep Radar Detector, 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.12187)).

Brodeski, Bilik, and Giryes introduced the *Deep Radar Detector*, the first framework to apply deep learning directly to complex radar data for a 4D detection task, relying on radar calibration data for supervision and proposing data-augmentation techniques tailored to radar ([Deep Radar Detector, 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.12187)).

They observed that "while camera and LiDAR processing have been revolutionized since the introduction of deep learning, radar processing still relies on classical tools" ([Deep Radar Detector, 2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.12187)).

CenterRadarNet extends this philosophy to 4D frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar, noting that "raw radio-frequency (RF) radar tensors contain rich spatiotemporal semantics" beyond what hand-engineered features preserve, and proposes joint 3D detection and tracking directly on these tensors ([CenterRadarNet, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01423)).

further argue that self-supervised learning on raw radar signals is essential because labeled radar data are scarce; their framework bootstraps representations from unlabeled raw radar ([Bootstrapping Autonomous Driving Radars, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04519)).

demonstrated that RD maps can be fed directly to a deep network for automotive target detection, framing the problem as a classical signal-processing regression task recast as a learning problem ([Range-Doppler Detection with Deep Learning, 2020](http://vigir.ee.missouri.edu/~gdesouza/Research/Conference_CDs/IEEE_WCCI_2020/IJCNN/Papers/N-21054.pdf)).

A subsequent contribution, the CRUW3D dataset, extends this line of work by providing 66K synchronized camera–radar–LiDAR frames for cross-modal learning ([RODNet/CRUW3D entry, Semantic Scholar](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/RODNet%3A-Radar-Object-Detection-using-Cross-Modal-Wang-Jiang/3b858058c04da3871848b81e8d8304e24c1282d5)).

The authors observe that "the common practice to summarize information in raw RAD data by reducing 3D information in the signal to 2D planes via averaging" tends to downgrade segmentation performance, and propose architectures that mitigate this loss while remaining computationally efficient ([ERASE-Net, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.12940)).

As there is no elevation information, it is challenging to estimate the 3D bounding box of an object from 3DRT" ([K-Radar, NeurIPS 2022](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/185fdf627eaae2abab36205dcd19b817-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html)).

CenterRadarNet builds directly on this 4D tensor paradigm, exploiting the elevation dimension for joint detection and tracking with 4D FMCW radar ([CenterRadarNet, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01423)).

The doctoral work of Dong explicitly motivates camera–radar fusion by noting that "the camera can capture rich semantic information, while radar has reliable ranging and speed estimation capability," and develops a 3D object perception strategy that consumes radar points in 3D space ([UW dissertation, 2023](https://digital.lib.washington.edu/researchworks/items/584e2f40-e50a-4284-8bf2-97c92df3d71d)).

GET-UP (2024) introduces a geometry-aware radar-point upsampling method, observing that naïvely projecting radar points onto the image plane produces a sparse depth map and that learned upsampling significantly improves depth estimation accuracy ([GET-UP, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02720)).

A complementary direction, presented in the 2024 *Camera–Radar Fusion with Modality Interaction and Radar Gaussian* work, treats radar points as Gaussian primitives in the fusion space, arguing that this representation is more robust to the inherent positional uncertainty of radar returns than treating each detection as a hard pixel-level measurement ([Camera–Radar Fusion with Radar Gaussian, 2024](https://spj.science.org/doi/pdf/10.34133/cbsystems.0079)).

PolarNet, introduced by Nowruzi et al., performs open-space segmentation directly in the polar domain, exploiting the fact that "the natural acquisition geometry of FMCW radar is polar" so that no costly range–azimuth reprojection is required before learning ([PolarNet, 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03387)).

The CRAFT architecture for camera–radar 3D object detection also operates in the polar coordinate system, observing that "image proposal with radar points in the polar coordinate system" efficiently handles the discrepancy between coordinate systems of the two modalities ([CRAFT, 2023](https://underline.io/lecture/69109-craft-camera-radar-3d-object-detection-with-spatio-contextual-fusion-transformer)).

Dong, Zhuang, Mao, and Liu (XSense.ai) introduced *Radar Camera Fusion via Representation Learning* in 2021, which is among the first works to formulate camera–radar fusion as a representation-learning problem rather than a rule-based projection, exploiting the fact that "radars and cameras are mature, cost-effective, and robust sensors … widely used in the perception stack of mass-produced autonomous driving systems" ([Radar Camera Fusion, 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07825)).

The CRAFT model extends this idea with a spatio-contextual fusion transformer that adaptively exchanges features between the two modalities through cross-attention layers ([CRAFT, 2023](https://underline.io/lecture/69109-craft-camera-radar-3d-object-detection-with-spatio-contextual-fusion-transformer)).

proposed a *Cross-Domain Spatial Matching* (CDSM) method for camera–radar fusion that explicitly addresses the geometric mismatch between the dense image grid and the sparse radar cloud, achieving improved object matching on the NuScenes benchmark ([Cross-Domain Spatial Matching, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16548)).

The 2024 *Camera–Radar Fusion with Modality Interaction and Radar Gaussian* work similarly emphasizes that the *form* of the radar representation—Gaussians, points, or heat-maps—directly affects the quality of the fused 3D object estimates ([Camera–Radar Fusion with Radar Gaussian, 2024](https://spj.science.org/doi/pdf/10.34133/cbsystems.0079)).

propose a self-supervised framework that learns radar representations from large amounts of unlabeled raw radar, then transfers them to downstream tasks such as detection ([Bootstrapping Autonomous Driving Radars, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04519)).

GET-UP shows that geometry-aware radar-point upsampling can serve as an auxiliary representation learning objective that improves depth estimation performance without any additional labels ([GET-UP, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02720)).
